candidateRows: Paul's early undisputed letters clearly attest his belief in Christ's bodily resurrection and appearances.
This establishes the earliest-source foundation of the affirmative resurrection case and directly addresses a principal component of the motion.
Albrecht proposes beginning with the early Pauline corpus and argues that its limited detail nevertheless establishes bodily resurrection belief and an appearance to Paul.
Paul's early letters permit a visionary interpretation and do not establish a bodily encounter with a resurrected person.
This directly contests whether the earliest Christian evidence supports bodily resurrection rather than an internally experienced vision.
Albrecht's claim that Paul's early letters clearly attest a bodily resurrection and bodily appearance.
Oppy distinguishes lying from visionary experience, argues that the letters do not specify an encounter between bodies, and denies that a vision proves an earlier resurrection.
The physical-body and spiritual-body language in First Corinthians 15 describes a tangible transformed body, not an immaterial entity.
The proposed linguistic reading supplies the affirmative side's textual basis for treating Paul's resurrection proclamation as bodily.
Oppy's contention that First Corinthians 15 can be read as visionary and does not describe a meeting of bodies.
Albrecht says his reading rests on First Corinthians 15 itself, including its Greek body terminology, while acknowledging and rejecting competing immaterial interpretations.
Paul's testimony about other resurrection witnesses is secondhand, and inherited reports could have shaped his interpretation of a visionary episode.
This challenges both the independence of Paul's experience and the reliability of the witness tradition used to support the resurrection.
Albrecht's reliance on Paul's writings and appearance claims as early evidence for bodily resurrection.
Oppy separates Paul's own experience from reports about the other witnesses and argues that those reports may have supplied the interpretive framework for whatever Paul experienced.
Known scribal interpolation creates uncertainty about how reliably unavailable source materials were copied into surviving Christian texts.
The move supplies a general textual-transmission objection to treating surviving scriptural wording as secure access to original testimony.
Albrecht's appeal to scriptural distinctions between visions and bodily appearances as historically reliable evidence.
Oppy notes that comparison exposes some later additions but argues that texts lacking earlier versions leave unresolved questions about their sources and copying history.
The decades between the reported events and the Gospels leave their sources, transmission reliability, and authorial selection uncertain.
This attacks the historical credibility of Gospel transmission, one of the motion's expressly identified foundations for the resurrection case.
Albrecht's defense of New Testament textual integrity and the general reliability of surviving manuscript traditions.
Oppy emphasizes the generational interval before Gospel composition and argues that even a self-described historian leaves unknown the sources used and the principles governing inclusion.
Early Pauline testimony, patristic reports, and hostile pagan descriptions jointly identify an early resurrection-believing orthodox Christian community.
This integrates early writings, hostile witnesses, and continuity claims into a cumulative affirmative case matching several components of the motion.
Oppy's claim that Gospel sources are unidentified and separated from the events by an unreliable transmission interval.

Albrecht appeals to patristic testimony about Gospel sources, the earlier date of Paul, and hostile descriptions whose identity markers allegedly correspond to scriptural rather than Gnostic Christianity.
Before the councils there were numerous competing Christian groups, and no determinate orthodoxy existed until councils defined it.
This directly denies the proposed continuity between earliest Christianity and later Catholic orthodoxy, another central component of the motion.
Albrecht's claim that early hostile sources distinguish a historically continuous orthodox group from competing Christian movements.
Oppy characterizes the first centuries as religiously plural and argues that labeling one stream orthodox before conciliar settlement projects a later category backward.
Surviving evidence may reflect preservation by later winners, making an absence of early theological diversity historically implausible.
This offers a selection-bias explanation for the affirmative continuity evidence and weakens inferences drawn from the present documentary record.
Albrecht's argument that the surviving pre-Nicene record shows continuity and little evidence of genuinely competing theologies.
Oppy argues that contrary materials may have disappeared or been destroyed and that the abundant later emergence of heresies makes uniformity before the councils unlikely.
Apparently untampered anti-Christian writings may have survived selectively because their contents were useful to later Christian preservers.
This directly rebuts the claim that uncontested hostile sources independently demonstrate widespread early orthodoxy by proposing documentary selection effects.
Albrecht's claim that uncontested hostile writings are credible because they show no signs of Christian interpolation or extensive doctrinal embellishment.

Oppy distinguishes preservation bias from tampering, infers that much ancient criticism disappeared during manuscript-selection decisions, and proposes that the surviving pagan evidence is unrepresentative.
A first-century hierarchy of bishops, priests, and deacons persisted through pre-Nicene disputes and supports continuity with the Catholic Church.
This directly advances the motion's central claim that early church structures provide historical grounds for Catholic continuity despite internal conflict.
The earlier skeptical question asked what pagan evidence supports widespread orthodoxy before the councils.
After denying that early Christianity was widespread, Albrecht argues that New Testament offices and their historical persistence identify a structured church founded by Jesus.
The early Christians remained a Jewish sect for a time, and limited knowledge of the diaspora and differing Syrian churches undercuts confidence in a simple continuity account.
The move resists the proposed linear Catholic institutional history by stressing uncertainty, changing Roman classification, and divergent early Christian communities.
Albrecht had proposed a continuous hierarchical church extending from the New Testament through Nicaea.
Oppy declines to affirm the proposed historical assessment, notes that Christians initially remained Jews in Roman eyes, and raises the existence of distinct Syrian Christianity.
Syriac and Roman churches are substantially aligned in Christology, Trinitarian theology, and Marian belief despite linguistic and political divisions.
The claimed doctrinal convergence answers an important challenge from diverse ancient churches and supports a historically unified core of apostolic orthodoxy.
Oppy had cited the Syrian Christian Church as an early community rather different from Rome.
Albrecht distinguishes verbal or stylistic difference from substantive theology, attributes much separation to later conflict, and argues for at least a fourth-century unified orthodoxy.
Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and Syriac churches share essential doctrines and councils, with the papacy as their principal major division.
This supports Catholic continuity by locating substantial doctrinal and conciliar unity across ancient apostolic churches despite incomplete institutional uniformity.
Oppy redirected the discussion to the more famous Great Schism between Eastern Orthodoxy and Catholicism.
Albrecht contrasts the papal dispute with broad agreement on Eucharistic doctrine, Trinity, Christology, and seven councils, then contrasts apostolic churches with evangelicalism.
The Reformation became more than an internal schism because Luther and later Protestant systems produced new, mutually divided religions.
The contrast between ancient apostolic continuity and later Protestant fragmentation is used to define the claimed boundaries of historical Catholic continuity.
Oppy asked whether Albrecht regarded the Reformation as something more extensive than a schism.
Albrecht allows that Luther may initially have intended reform but argues that theological transformation and later Protestant disagreement yielded separate religious systems.
Numerous medieval movements sought church reform before Luther, so reformist criticism and concern about clerical corruption were not uniquely Reformation phenomena.
The historical counterexample complicates the proposed sharp boundary between continuous Catholic reform and an unprecedented Protestant departure.
Albrecht had characterized Luther's movement as creating an entirely different and internally divided religion.
Oppy points to earlier reform movements concerned with changing the church and combating clerical corruption, challenging an overly abrupt account of the Reformation break.
Earlier reform groups retained characteristic Catholic doctrines, whereas Luther's movement shed those doctrines and ultimately became a different religion.
This historical comparison is offered to defend a continuous Catholic doctrinal identity while explaining why Protestantism represents discontinuity rather than ordinary reform.
Oppy had observed that medieval reform movements and anticorruption efforts substantially preceded Luther.
Albrecht concedes earlier reform efforts but says groups such as the Waldensians retained Eucharistic, Marian, purgatorial, and devotional teachings later discarded in Protestantism.
Catholic and Orthodox theology remains substantially compatible despite popular hostility, differing language, and disagreement over doctrines such as purgatory or the Immaculate Conception.
The move strengthens the continuity thesis by arguing that apparent Catholic-Orthodox distance does not erase shared theology and apostolic ecclesial status.
Oppy questioned whether Albrecht's Greek Orthodox acquaintances would accept his claim that the churches are close.
Albrecht acknowledges that many Orthodox believers perceive a wide gulf, but cites scholarly and doctrinal compatibility and describes Orthodoxy as possessing valid apostolic orders.
Catholics and Orthodox share early Greek fathers and broad apostolic inheritance, while their recognized saints diverge principally after later institutional conflicts.
Shared patristic authorities furnish historical support for a common early tradition, while later differences are presented as bounded consequences of subsequent schism.
Oppy asked what division besides the papacy could be sufficiently large to separate Catholics and Orthodox.
Albrecht emphasizes shared Mariology and early fathers, then uses Mark of Ephesus and the Council of Florence to locate later divergence over anti-Roman figures.
Protestant traditions are better classified as branches of Christianity because they retain scripture and history in common, and religious individuation is inherently difficult.
This directly challenges the Catholic argument that Protestant diversity constitutes wholly different religions and weakens that contrast as evidence for exclusive Catholic continuity.
Albrecht asked whether the Reformation was merely a schism or a branching into completely new religions.
Oppy argues that large internal differences do not prevent Catholicism and Protestantism from belonging to Christianity, then compares broader Abrahamic and Eastern classifications.
